title: Late have I loved thee (Confessions 10.27)
hookLine: too late loved I thee, O thou Beauty of ancient days, yet ever new

lines: BOOK TEN: WHO HE IS NOW.
cards: Late. It's a word with a sting in it. Late for the train.
Late with the apology. Too late to say it to someone who's gone. In book ten of the Confessions, Augustine has finished telling the story of his past and turns to who he is now.
Partway through, the word he reaches for is that one. Late. Read on a few lines, though, and it isn't a cry of despair.
It turns into something closer to a love letter.

teach.b: First, the opening, in Edward Pusey's old English translation: "Too late loved I Thee, O Thou Beauty of ancient days, yet ever new! too late I loved Thee!"
In Augustine's Latin: sero te amavi, pulchritudo tam antiqua et tam nova. Beauty so ancient and so new. God isn't called judge here, or king.
God is called beauty, older than anything and fresh as this morning. Second, where he'd been looking.

teach.h: YOU WERE WITHIN; I WAS OUTSIDE.
teach.b: You were within, he says, and I was outside, and there I searched for you. He'd hunted through the lovely things God had made, as if they were the end of the road.
Then one short line: "Thou wert with me, but I was not with Thee." The distance was never on God's side.

teach.h: SENSE BY SENSE, GOD BREAKS IN.
teach.b: Third, how God broke through, sense by sense. You called and shouted, and broke through my deafness. You flashed and shone, and scattered my blindness.
You breathed fragrance, and I drew in my breath and now I long for you. I tasted, and now I hunger and thirst. You touched me, and I burned for your peace.
The same senses that had kept him busy outside become the way God reaches him. Fourth, why late isn't the last word. He says late twice; he doesn't pretend the lost years away.
But everything after it is about being found.
It's the honest start of a love already under way.

how: Catholics hear this passage from the Confessions in the Office of Readings on the feast of Saint Augustine, and some pray its lines on their own.

o: Latin for beauty, Augustine's name for God
Latin for lateness, as in late have I loved
Latin for the soul's longing for heaven

games.q: late have I loved thee — tap the pairs.

s: in this passage Augustine calls God beauty
"O Thou Beauty of ancient days, yet ever new."
Augustine says God was far away from him
"Thou wert with me, but I was not with Thee." the distance was on his side.
the senses are only a distraction in this passage
God reaches him through hearing, sight, smell, taste and touch.

games.q: you're Augustine, looking for beauty everywhere outside yourself. where does the passage say God was the whole time?
games.why: "you were within, and I was outside," he says. he'd been searching everywhere except where God already was.

practice: Go through the senses the way Augustine does: one sound in the room, one patch of light, one smell, even if it's only the air, one taste, and one place where something touches you, a chair, your sleeve.
Don't chase them; let each one be a door. If you pray, say Augustine's words slowly, once: too late loved I thee, O thou beauty of ancient days, yet ever new.

wordCard.voice: pulchritudo. Latin for beauty, what Augustine called God in Confessions ten: a beauty so ancient, and so new. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: late have I loved thee — the opening of Confessions 10.27.

carryVoice: Your line: ever ancient, ever new. The beauty he found late had been with him all along. Day seven hundred thirty-eight, done.
